crime.value: Murder by stabbing. Wesley Schmidt, a Pinkerton detective posing as a waiter, is killed with a switch knife in his car in Bloodfield (Southwest DC). Central question: Will the narrator's involvement be discovered, or will police blame a Black suspect in the neighborhood?
crime.quote: I brought the knife across real fast and buried it into his armpit...His blood came out like someone was pouring it from a jug.

victim.value: Wesley Schmidt, a Pinkerton detective hired to infiltrate the restaurant and investigate labor organizing meetings. He is 'killable' because he is an enforcer of capital; he likely murdered John Petersen (the narrator's friend) to suppress union activity, making him a threat the narrator must neutralize.
victim.quote: I'm telling you, Schmidt is no waiter...Don't ever mention those meetings again, to anyone...Do you know what a Pinkerton man is?

closed_world.value: The restaurant on 15th and Penn Avenue where the narrator works as a busman, and the broader Greek immigrant community in Washington DC (Chinatown, church, coffeehouses). Schmidt's car in Bloodfield (Southwest DC) serves as the immediate crime scene.
closed_world.quote: The hotel was pretty fancy...I worked at St. Mary's...the coffeehouses down by the Navy Yard in Southeast.

culprit_and_motive.value: The narrator (Bill/Vasili), a Greek immigrant busman. Motive: Revenge for John Petersen's murder and self-defense against a Pinkerton operative who represents capitalist suppression of labor organizing. Schmidt's boasting about manipulating workers ('they're like children') and his presence at union meetings made him a lethal threat.
culprit_and_motive.quote: Pretty hard to swim, you got a bullet in your head...I just wanna know what happened to John.

resolution.value: No formal resolution. The crime remains unsolved. Police will likely blame a Black resident of Bloodfield. The narrator expects either capture (if Raymond the cook testifies) or freedom. He plans to continue his life—save money, open a restaurant, marry Irene—while living under the shadow of unresolved consequences.
resolution.quote: They're gonna find Schmidt in that neighborhood and they're gonna figure a colored guy killed him for his money...If Raymond tells them he saw me I'm gonna get the chair. If he doesn't, I'm gonna be free.

investigator.value: The narrator himself—Bill/Vasili, the Greek immigrant busman. The reader experiences the mystery through his first-person confession/reflection. He is simultaneously perpetrator, investigator (seeking truth about John's death), and potential suspect awaiting discovery.
investigator.quote: SOMEDAY I'M GONNA write all this down...Last night I had a dream...This is where I am right now.

suspect_architecture.value: Single perpetrator (Vasili/Bill) and one victim (Schmidt). Schmidt is framed as a Pinkerton informant; Raymond the cook is a potential witness who could implicate or exonerate. No traditional multi-suspect spread — the architecture inverts convention by centering the killer as narrator.
suspect_architecture.quote: If Raymond tells them he saw me I'm gonna get the chair. If he doesn't, I'm gonna be free.

red_herring.value: Vasili lures Schmidt with a fabricated whorehouse tip, misdirecting Schmidt (and initially the reader) about the purpose of the night drive. Separately, the murder scene is designed to make police believe a Black resident of Bloodfield killed Schmidt for robbery — a deliberate racial frame-up.
red_herring.quote: They're gonna find Schmidt in that neighborhood and they're gonna figure a colored guy killed him for his money.

clue_fairness.value: The story is first-person confession, so reader and narrator share identical information throughout. Blood under Vasili's fingernails is shown to the reader on page one, before any explanation is given — a classic fair-play plant that retrospectively confirms the killing.
clue_fairness.quote: I got blood underneath my fingernails. I washed real good but it was hard to get it all.

social_world.value: Depression-era Washington D.C. ethnic immigrant underclass (Greek, Italian, Irish, Polish) stratified against Anglo establishment. Labor organizing is suppressed by Pinkerton infiltrators; racial hierarchy marginalizes Black workers like Raymond. Debt, patronage, and ethnic loyalty networks govern mobility.
social_world.quote: Toula's father owed my father some lefta from back in the village, so it was all set up.

alibi.value: No formal alibi is constructed by Vasili. Instead, the racial geography of Bloodfield functions as a structural alibi — police are expected to assume a Black suspect, deflecting investigation away from Vasili entirely. Schmidt's Pinkerton cover identity is itself a kind of institutional alibi.
alibi.quote: They're gonna turn Bloodfield upside down.

reveal_mechanic.value: The reveal is embedded in the opening frame: blood under the narrator's nails and the pre-dawn setting are disclosed before the backstory, so the confession structure itself is the mechanic — the reader assembles causation retroactively as Vasili narrates forward to the present moment.
reveal_mechanic.quote: Let me go back some, to show how I got to where I am tonight.

media_and_audience.value: John Petersen's death received only a brief Tribune notice with no follow-up, demonstrating how institutional media erases inconvenient working-class deaths. Vasili expects Schmidt's murder will be similarly misreported as a robbery, relying on press and police indifference to Black neighborhoods.
media_and_audience.quote: It was just a short notice, and it didn't say nothing else.

investigator_wound.value: Vasili is simultaneously perpetrator and investigator of John Petersen's murder. His wound is grief, displacement, and impotent rage at being powerless within American systems — the killing of Schmidt is the only justice available to him, at the cost of his last link to Greece (his father's knife).
investigator_wound.quote: I was crying 'cause my father had given me that knife, and now it was gone.

_meta.title: The	Dead	Their	Eyes	Implore	Us
_meta.author: GEORGE	P.	PELECANOS
